cells.quote: Reading achievement. Calderón, Hertz-Lazarowitz, and Slavin (1998) found statistically significant differences between the English language learners who participated in the BCIRC program and students in the comparison group.6 The WWC analysis, however, could not confirm the statistical significance of this finding because it was necessary to correct for clustering. The size of the effect was large enough to be considered substantively important, however, so the intervention in this study had potentially positive effects on reading achievement, according to WWC standards.
cells.note: The study was a quasi-experimental design with reservations; the WWC classified the corrected result as not statistically significant but substantively important.

cells.quote: However, the findings for students who had been involved with the intervention for one year became nonsignificant after correcting for clustering.

O.outcome_detail: Implementation of differentiated-instruction strategies in classroom practice

cells.quote: By integrating micro-credentials into the “Learning Differences” MOOC-Ed, the Friday Institute was able to engage hundreds of educators with rich, well-researched best practices and guide their implementation of strategies into actual classroom practice — all at scale.
cells.note: Narrative case report; no quantitative comparison, random assignment, or effect size is reported.

O.outcome_detail: Skill-based implementation of district-priority instructional practices

cells.quote: Micro-credentials provided BCPS educators with a more complete way to grow and meet the professional demands of leading their students. “Micro-credentials selected for our pilot expanded PD offerings around district initiatives where growth is taking place and also filled gaps not covered by our workshops. Say, something specific like using exit tickets effectively – we don’t necessarily cover that topic in individual workshops. Micro-credentials dig into one specific piece of instruction,” according to Amanda Lanza, Specialist in the Office of Digital Learning.
cells.note: The report describes a 2015–2016 pilot but does not report a formal comparison or measured outcome.

O.outcome_detail: Educator empowerment and ownership of professional learning

cells.quote: “You’re really responsible for learning on your own with micro-credentials. It’s very, very different than any other PD. The element of implementation being put on the educator was very different — in a good way. It was empowering,” according to Jennifer Madrid, S.T.A.T. teacher at the Rosedale Center, an alternative 6-12 school in BCPS.
cells.note: This direction is based on a participant quotation in a narrative case study, not on a validated motivation measure.

D.treatment: micro-credentials linked to classroom evidence and reflection
D.comparison: professional development without this implementation pathway

O.outcome_detail: Transfer of professional-development content into classroom action

cells.quote: The truth of the matter is that even with great professional development, the multiple demands on an educator make it challenging to transfer PD content into action in the classroom. However, as educators produce evidence of competence through classroom artifacts in the micro-credential process, they are incentivized to apply their learning in their day-to-day work.
cells.note: The report presents a proposed mechanism and narrative claim; it does not provide a measured treatment-versus-comparison estimate.

cells.quote: Further analysis of these data alongside federal English Learner program data illustrated that in many cases school districts with above average BCLAD-authorized staff had below-average bilingual program enrollment and vice versa. This suggests that the supply of these staff could be more effectively aligned with current demand for these programs.
cells.note: The study reports a measured association between BCLAD-authorized staff levels and bilingual program enrollment; it provides no printed effect size.
